The Main Thing

We can get 3x the performance if we migrate this to Rust

A TypeScript Compiler Journey from Hell

It’s only been 3 months since TypeScript 7 aka “the Go port” came out, which was supposed to solve all of our TypeScript perf problems. But in the last few weeks, we’ve had not one, not two, not three, but four “slop ports” of the compiler, which is proof that we’ve reached the 7th level of hell.

And while it’s hard to focus with the weeping and gnashing of teeth, I suppose it’s fair to ask the question: why is everyone porting the compiler?

How did we get here:

When TypeScript migrated to Go, they shipped a native binary that made the compiler run faster, but it meant tools depending on its old JavaScript API could no longer call it directly. Instead, they had to talk to it over a client/server protocol, leaving the tooling ecosystem somewhat fragmented. When you combine this with a Rust fetish and unlimited tokens, it isn’t hard to see why it’s forking season.

The pitchforks:

  • tsc-rs: Theo’s influencer token budget brought forth the original “experimental” port, ts-rust, which can type-check the entire VS Code codebase in 4.8 seconds, compared with 9.6 seconds for the Go version.

  • bun check: Bun aka “the slop father” also ported the TypeScript compiler and embedded it into their toolkit, making type checks 3–6.4x faster while using 2.2–4.9x less memory in Bun’s benchmarks.

  • tsc-ts: Perhaps the most interesting fork was Vercel Labs deciding to migrate the compiler BACK to TypeScript and compile it to native using scriptc, delivering similar performance to the Go version.

  • tsrs: Not wanting to be left out, the VoidZero team at Cloudflare announced they will be maintaining a new project called tsrs, a Rust port they plan to merge with Theo’s port and integrate it into the Oxc toolchain.

Bottom Line: In the slopfork ecosystem, when you outsource original ideas for more control, projects like these can start to feel pretty boring. But what did you expect… we’re in hell after all.

Spot the Bug

Spot the Bug – Presented by Trigger.dev

Trigger.dev is an open-source platform for building durable AI agents and workflows in TypeScript. If steps fail, processes restart, or code deploys mid-run, your tasks pick up where they left off instead of dying.

function flattenArray(arr) {
  let result = [];
  arr.forEach((item) => {
    if (Array.isArray(item)) {
      result.concat(flattenArray(item));
    } else {
      result.push(item);
    }
  });
  return result;
}

console.log(flattenArray([1, [2, [3, [4]]]]));

Spot the Bug: Solution

Spot the Bug – Presented by Trigger.dev

Array.prototype.concat() doesn’t mutate the original array; it returns a new array. To fix the issue, we need to assign the return value of result.concat(flattenArray(item)) back to result.

function flattenArray(arr) {
  let result = [];
  arr.forEach((item) => {
    if (Array.isArray(item)) {
      result = result.concat(flattenArray(item));
    } else {
      result.push(item);
    }
  });
  return result;
}

console.log(flattenArray([1, [2, [3, [4]]]]));
